# Reproducible Reports with Quarto {#sec-quarto}

A number read off the console and typed into a sentence takes four
seconds, and it is the most reasonable thing in the world to do.
It also severs the connection between the analysis and the claim.
On the day the data are corrected and the analysis is re-run, the
figures update and the sentence does not, and nothing anywhere
tells you so. Literate programming closes that gap: the sentence
carries the code that computes its number, so the number cannot
drift from the analysis. Quarto is the current tool for doing this
in R, and most of this chapter is about the few places where it
can still let a stale number through.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```

of programs: instead of imagining that our main task is to
instruct a computer what to do, let us concentrate rather on
explaining to human beings what we want a computer to do.*

[Donald E. Knuth]{.smallcaps}, *Literate Programming* (1984)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

## Literate programming and the inline number {#sec-quarto-literate}

Donald Knuth's idea [@knuth1984literate] was that source code and
prose should live in one document, with the prose explaining the
code as one person would explain it to another. Quarto implements
it with code chunks and prose interleaved in a `.qmd` file. The
part that matters most for a statistician is the smallest: an
inline expression, which puts a computed value inside a sentence.

````qmd
We compared the 30-day composite outcome between the randomized
arms.

```{{r}}
obs <- trial[!is.na(trial$event_30d), ]
rates <- tapply(obs$event_30d, obs$arm, mean)
```

Readmission or death within 30 days occurred in
`{{r}} round(100 * rates[["Usual care"]], 1)`% of patients
under usual care.
````

Rendering runs the chunk, evaluates the inline expression, and
writes its value into the sentence. Re-render after the data change
and the sentence changes with them. Copying the number into Word
instead is where 'I forgot to update Table 2' comes from.

What to compute inline is the author's decision, and the rule is
simple: any number that depends on the data. That includes the
sample size in the abstract, the count of exclusions in the
methods, every estimate and interval, and the p-value that a
reviewer will check against the table. A manuscript with
`p < 0.05` typed into it is correct only until the next extract.

### The minimum document

````qmd
---
title: "HF-HOME interim summary"
format: html
---

Some prose here.

```{{r}}
1 + 1
```
````

Save it as `analysis.qmd` and render it from the shell with
`quarto render analysis.qmd`, which writes `analysis.html`. The
`format:` key decides the output; with none, Quarto writes HTML.
One source can produce several formats, which keeps a single
source of truth for the website, the journal, and the collaborator
who edits only in Word, at the price of the constraints in
@tbl-quarto-formats.

| Format | Command | What it cannot carry |
|---|---|---|
| HTML | `quarto render analysis.qmd --to html` | Nothing that matters here; it is the most capable target |
| PDF | `quarto render analysis.qmd --to pdf` | Interactive HTML widgets; needs a LaTeX installation (`quarto install tinytex`) |
| Word | `quarto render analysis.qmd --to docx` | Fine typographic control; LaTeX math is converted and may need checking |

: One source, three outputs. List several formats under `format:`
to render them all at once. {#tbl-quarto-formats}

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your manuscript says 'The mean age was 67.3 years
(SD 12.1)', typed in from the console. What is wrong with this, and
what is the Quarto fix?

**Answer.** The numbers are detached from the data. Re-run the
analysis on corrected data and the prose still says 67.3 and 12.1,
while every table beside it has moved. The fix is inline
computation:

```qmd
The mean age was `{{r}} round(mean(d$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`
years (SD `{{r}} round(sd(d$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`).
```

The prose is now computed at render time, so a re-render on new
data updates it. It is still possible for the rendered document to
be stale, if the code was not re-run; @sec-quarto-freeze is about
when that happens.
:::

### Exercises

1. Write the sentence 'The mean age at index discharge was X years
   (SD Y), and Z patients were older than 89' for the HF-HOME
   demographics file
   (`file.path('..', 'data', 'raw_data', 'hfhome', 'demographics.csv')`),
   with every number inline. Compute the values in a chunk so that
   you can check the rendered sentence against them.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The sentence, with its setup chunk:

````qmd
```{{r}}
#| include: false
demo <- read.csv(file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome",
                           "demographics.csv"),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
```

The mean age at index discharge was
`{{r}} round(mean(demo$age), 1)` years
(SD `{{r}} round(sd(demo$age), 1)`), and
`{{r}} sum(demo$age > 89)` patients were older than 89.
````

The values it should render:

```{r}
#| label: soln-11-1
demo <- read.csv(file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome",
                           "demographics.csv"),
                 colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
c(mean = round(mean(demo$age), 1), sd = round(sd(demo$age), 1),
  over_89 = sum(demo$age > 89))
```

The count of patients over 89 matters beyond this chapter: ages
above 89 are an identifier under the HIPAA (Health Insurance
Portability and Accountability Act) Safe Harbor method
(@sec-deident), so a de-identified extract would not let you
compute it, and the sentence would have to change.
:::

## Chunks, cross-references, and citations {#sec-quarto-chunks}

### Chunk options

A chunk's options sit at its top, one per line after `#|`:

````qmd
```{{r}}
#| label: fig-outcome-by-arm
#| fig-cap: "30-day readmission or death by randomized arm"
#| fig-width: 6
#| echo: false

ggplot(obs, aes(arm, fill = factor(event_30d))) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")
```
````

| Option | Effect | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `echo: false` | Runs the code, shows the output, hides the code | Papers; keep `true` for teaching and review |
| `include: false` | Runs the code, shows nothing | Setup chunks that read data and load packages |
| `eval: false` | Shows the code, does not run it | Code that must not execute, such as a deployment command |
| `warning: false`, `message: false` | Suppresses warnings or messages | A chunk whose warnings you have read and judged harmless |
| `label: fig-...` | Names the chunk and makes it a cross-reference target | Every figure and table you refer to |
| `fig-cap`, `fig-width`, `fig-height` | Caption and size of the figure | Every figure |
| `cache: true` | Reuses the chunk's stored result (@sec-quarto-freeze) | An expensive chunk in a single document |

: Chunk options in common use. {#tbl-quarto-chunk-options}

The front matter is the YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) header
between the `---` lines at the top of the file. Set defaults for
every chunk under its `execute:` key, for example `echo: false`,
and override them per chunk.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A global `warning: false` hides the warnings that make failures
loud.** `dplyr`'s many-to-many join warning (@sec-joins), `glm()`'s
'fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1', and a date parser's
'failed to parse' are each the only sign of a wrong number, and
with `warning: false` set under `execute:` none of them reaches
the rendered document, where a reader would see it. Leave warnings
on while the analysis is changing, and suppress them per chunk,
after you have read them.
:::

### Cross-references

Label a figure, table, equation, or section, and refer to it by
label; Quarto numbers it and writes 'Figure 3' or a link.

````qmd
See @fig-outcome-by-arm for the outcome by arm.

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-outcome-by-arm
#| fig-cap: "30-day readmission or death by randomized arm"
ggplot(obs, aes(arm, fill = factor(event_30d))) + geom_bar()
```
````

| Prefix | Labels | Where the label goes |
|---|---|---|
| `fig-` | Figures | The chunk's `label:` option |
| `tbl-` | Tables | The chunk's `label:`, or `{#tbl-...}` after a pipe table's caption |
| `eq-` | Equations | `{#eq-...}` after the closing `$$` |
| `sec-` | Sections | `{#sec-...}` after the heading, as in `# Methods {#sec-methods}` |

: Cross-reference prefixes. {#tbl-quarto-xref}

The same source produces hyperlinks in HTML, numbered references
in PDF, and field codes in Word.

### Citations

Point the front matter at a BibTeX file and a citation style, and
cite by key:

```yaml
bibliography: references.bib
csl: https://www.zotero.org/styles/jama
```

```qmd
This builds on prior work [@bryan2019happygit; @marwick2018rrtools].
@wickham2019advr discusses copy-on-modify in detail.
```

`[@key]` gives a parenthetical citation and `@key` a textual one;
separate several keys with semicolons. The CSL (Citation Style
Language) file sets the journal's format, so changing journals
means changing one line. Start the `.bib` file on the first day:
backfilling the citations of a finished draft is slow, and a
methods section whose references were typed by hand cannot be
reformatted or checked.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You write `@fig-trajectory` in the prose, but the
chunk that should produce the figure is display-only, so the label
never exists. What happens when you render, and why is that better
than writing 'Figure 3'?

**Answer.** Quarto prints `WARN: Unable to resolve crossref
@fig-trajectory` and renders the reference as `?@fig-trajectory`.
The build completes, but the defect is visible in the log and in
the output. Written as 'Figure 3', the reference is a string:
insert a figure earlier and the sentence points at the wrong one,
with nothing to warn you. Cross-references turn the errors that
revision introduces into build warnings, as inline code does for
numbers.
:::

### Exercises

2. Convert a short `.R` script of yours into a `.qmd` that renders
   to both HTML and PDF, with one captioned figure, one
   cross-reference to it, and one citation from a `.bib` file.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A correct result renders both formats without a `WARN` line,
shows 'Figure 1' (or a link) where you wrote the reference, and
ends with a reference list in both outputs. Two failures are
common. A reference rendered as `?@fig-...` means the label is
missing or misspelled, or the chunk did not run. A citation
rendered as its bare key, with a 'citation not found' warning,
means the key is not in the `.bib` file the front matter names.
If the PDF fails with a LaTeX error, run `quarto install tinytex`.
:::

## Freeze and cache {#sec-quarto-freeze}

A ten-second analysis can run on every render; a ten-minute
bootstrap or an MCMC (Markov chain Monte Carlo) fit cannot. Quarto
offers two ways to store a result and reuse it, and they differ in
scope, in what makes them re-run, and in when they are ignored
(@tbl-quarto-freeze-cache). The rule for both is to store a result
only when the computation is expensive *and* deterministic, and to
re-run anything that is cheap or could change.

| | `freeze` (Quarto) | `cache` (knitr) |
|---|---|---|
| Set with | `execute: freeze: auto` in `_quarto.yml` or a document's front matter | `cache: true` on a chunk, or under `execute:` |
| Scope | A whole document | One chunk |
| Applies | Only inside a Quarto project (a directory with `_quarto.yml`) | In any document |
| Stored in | `_freeze/` at the project root | A `<document>_cache/` directory beside the document |
| Re-executes when | `auto`: any change to the document's source, even one character, re-runs the whole document; `true`: never during a project render; `false` (the default): always | The chunk's code or options change |
| Ignored when | You render a single file or a subdirectory, which always executes | Never ignored by the kind of render |
| Does not notice | Changed data files, packages, or R version | Changed data files, packages, or upstream chunks (unless `dependson` names them) |
| Commit to Git? | Commonly, so that collaborators and automated builds reuse expensive results | Usually not |

: `freeze` and `cache` compared. {#tbl-quarto-freeze-cache}

The two consequences in the 'Ignored when' row catch people out.
`quarto render analysis.qmd` executes the document whatever
`freeze` says, so freeze speeds up only full project renders. And
a stand-alone `.qmd` outside any project has no `_freeze/` at all;
for chunk-level reuse there, use `cache: true`.

`_freeze/` can be committed to Git, so that a collaborator or a
continuous-integration (CI) build that renders the project reuses
the stored results instead of re-running a long analysis
(@sec-git-teams discusses the merge conflicts this can bring). The
stored results are whatever the last execution produced; a
randomized chunk that sets its own seed reproduces them when it
does re-run, and one that does not will produce different numbers
from the stored ones.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Neither `freeze` nor `cache` sees the data.** Both decide whether
to re-run by looking at code. Replace `data/trial.csv` with a new
extract and a project render under `freeze: auto` serves the old
numbers, with no warning, because the `.qmd` did not change; a
cached chunk that reads the file does the same. This is the
typed-number failure again, one level down, and the worked example
below shows it happening. After a data change, render the document
itself, or delete its entry in `_freeze/`. For a cached chunk, add
`cache.extra: !expr tools::md5sum("data/trial.csv")`, which makes
the file's checksum part of what the cache compares.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A project uses `freeze: auto`. You fix a typo in the
discussion of `results.qmd` and run `quarto render`. Which chunks
re-execute?

**Answer.** Every chunk in `results.qmd`, and none in any other
document. Freeze works per document, so any change to the source,
prose included, invalidates the whole document's stored results.
If you wanted only the expensive chunk protected, that is
`cache: true` on the chunk, whose key is the chunk's own code.
:::

### Exercises

3. For each scenario, say whether the code re-executes:
   (a) project render, `freeze: auto`, prose edited;
   (b) project render, `freeze: auto`, data file replaced;
   (c) `quarto render report.qmd` with `freeze: true`;
   (d) `cache: true` chunk, an upstream chunk edited;
   (e) `cache: true` chunk, its own code edited.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
| Scenario | Re-executes? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| (a) | Yes, the whole document | `auto` watches the source, and prose is source |
| (b) | No | Freeze does not see data files; the results are stale |
| (c) | Yes | A single-file render ignores `freeze` |
| (d) | No | The cache key is the chunk's own code; add `dependson` |
| (e) | Yes | The chunk's code is its cache key |

: Exercise 3 key. {#tbl-quarto-ex3}

Scenarios (b) and (d) are the dangerous ones, because each
produces a document that looks current.
:::

## Worked example: a report that survives a new extract {#sec-quarto-worked}

The example builds a one-paragraph HF-HOME report in a temporary
Quarto project with `freeze: auto`, renders it against an interim
extract, then replaces the data with the full extract and renders
it twice more. It runs the real `quarto` command, so the output
below is what you would see.[^quarto-env]

[^quarto-env]: The `env` argument passes this session's library
    paths to the R process that Quarto starts, so that it finds the
    same packages. In a terminal you would type `quarto render`
    alone.

```{r}
#| label: quarto-worked-setup
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
read_hf <- function(file) {
  read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
           colClasses = c(patient_id = "character"))
}
randomization <- read_hf("randomization.csv")
outcomes <- read_hf("outcomes.csv")
trial <- merge(
  randomization[c("patient_id", "site", "rand_date", "arm")],
  outcomes[c("patient_id", "event_30d")],
  by = "patient_id"
)
stopifnot(nrow(trial) == nrow(randomization),
          !anyDuplicated(trial$patient_id))

proj <- file.path(tempdir(), "hfhome-report")
unlink(proj, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(file.path(proj, "data"), recursive = TRUE)
writeLines(c("project:", "  type: default",
             "execute:", "  freeze: auto"),
           file.path(proj, "_quarto.yml"))
writeLines(c(
  '---',
  'title: "HF-HOME: 30-day outcomes by arm"',
  'format: gfm',
  '---',
  '',
  '```{r}',
  '#| include: false',
  'd <- read.csv("data/trial.csv")',
  'obs <- d[!is.na(d$event_30d), ]',
  'pct <- function(a) round(100 * mean(obs$event_30d[obs$arm == a]), 1)',
  '```',
  '',
  'Of `r nrow(d)` patients randomized, `r nrow(obs)` had the',
  'primary outcome ascertained. Readmission or death within 30',
  'days occurred in `r pct("Usual care")`% under usual care and',
  '`r pct("Home health")`% with home health.'
), file.path(proj, "report.qmd"))

render_report <- function(target, ...) {
  r_libs <- paste0("R_LIBS=",
                   paste(.libPaths(), collapse = .Platform$path.sep))
  status <- system2("quarto", c("render", target, ..., "--quiet"),
                    env = r_libs)
  stopifnot(status == 0)
  md <- readLines(file.path(proj, "report.md"))
  paste(md[nzchar(md)][-1], collapse = " ")
}
```

The report's inline expressions use the R Markdown spelling, a
backtick, `r`, and a space, which Quarto's knitr engine also
accepts.[^inline-spelling] In your own documents use the `{{r}}`
spelling shown earlier in the chapter.

[^inline-spelling]: Quarto rewrites every `{{r}}` inline expression
    in a document before any chunk runs, including one inside a
    string in a chunk. A chapter written in Quarto therefore cannot
    write that spelling into a file this way.

The interim extract holds the patients randomized by the end of
March 2025. Render the whole project, as a build script or CI would:

```{r}
#| label: quarto-worked-interim
interim <- trial[trial$rand_date <= "2025-03-31", ]
write.csv(interim, file.path(proj, "data", "trial.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
render_report(proj)
```

The full extract arrives. Replace the data file and render the
project again:

```{r}
#| label: quarto-worked-stale
write.csv(trial, file.path(proj, "data", "trial.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
stale <- render_report(proj)
stale
```

The paragraph has not changed. Every number in it is computed, and
every number is wrong, because `freeze: auto` saw an unchanged
`report.qmd` and served the stored results. Render the document
itself, which always executes:

```{r}
#| label: quarto-worked-current
current <- render_report(file.path(proj, "report.qmd"))
current
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Compute the counts independently of the report and confirm that
the current render states them and the stale one does not.

```{r}
#| label: quarto-worked-verify
obs <- trial[!is.na(trial$event_30d), ]
expected <- sprintf("Of %d patients randomized, %d had the",
                    nrow(trial), nrow(obs))
stopifnot(grepl(expected, current, fixed = TRUE),
          !grepl(expected, stale, fixed = TRUE))
expected
```

In your own project, the same check is a test (@sec-testing): read
the rendered output and assert that it contains the numbers the
analysis computes.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to convert typed numbers to inline code, and check the
result by changing the data.

> **Context.** Below are the data dictionary for `trial.csv`
> (`patient_id`, `site`, `rand_date`, `arm`, `event_30d`) and the
> results paragraph of a Quarto report whose setup chunk reads
> `data/trial.csv` into `d`. Every number in the paragraph was
> typed by hand.
>
> **Constraints.** Replace every number that depends on the data
> with an inline `{{r}}` expression computed from `d`, defining
> any helper objects in the setup chunk. Use base R. Do not change
> the wording, and do not write any data-dependent number as a
> literal, including denominators inside an expression.
>
> **Criteria.** List each number you replaced and the expression
> that now computes it. The document must render, and every number
> in the paragraph must change when it is rendered against a
> different extract.

*Failure mode.* The model computes a value itself and writes it
back as a literal, or writes `sum(d$event_30d) / 2432`, an inline
expression with a typed denominator that renders the right number
today and a wrong one on the next extract. *Check.* Render against
the interim and the full extracts, as above, and compare the two
paragraphs number by number
(`regmatches(x, gregexpr("[0-9.]+", x))` lists them); a number that
is the same in both is typed or must be justified. Then read each
listed expression for constants. A dictionary and a paragraph hold
no patient data, so they may go to any approved tool
(@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In the worked example, the stale render contained no
typed numbers. Why did it still report the interim results, and why
would no reviewer reading the output notice?

**Answer.** Inline code guarantees that a number is computed when
the document executes; it says nothing about whether the document
executed. `freeze: auto` skipped execution because the source was
unchanged, so the computed numbers were from the previous run.
The paragraph is internally consistent and plausible, which is
what makes it dangerous (Habit 8). A line in the report that
states which extract it used, as in Exercise 4, makes the
staleness visible.
:::

### Exercises

4. Add a sentence to the worked example's report that states the
   extract it was computed from, using the latest randomization
   date in `d`, so that a stale render announces itself.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```qmd
Computed from the extract of patients randomized through
`{{r}} max(d$rand_date)`.
```

The stale render in the worked example would then name a date in
March 2025 beside numbers the reader believes are final, which a
reader can catch. Stating provenance in the output is a cheap form
of the assertion habit: it does not prevent the stale render, but
it turns a silent failure into a visible one.
:::

## Parameterized reports {#sec-quarto-params}

A parameter lets one `.qmd` render against different inputs:
one report per site in a multi-site trial, per sensitivity
analysis, or per institution. Declare the parameter and its
default in the front matter, and read it as `params$site`:

```yaml
params:
  site: "All"
```

Render a variant from the shell (display-only):

```bash
quarto render report.qmd -P site:"Site C"
```

Or from R with the `quarto` package:

```r
quarto::quarto_render("report.qmd",
                      execute_params = list(site = "Site C"),
                      output_file = "report-site-c.html")
```

A parameterized report renders the *same* document against
*different* data; a website (@sec-quarto-reference) renders
*different* documents into one whole. A multi-site trial may use
both: one parameterized report per site, collected into a site
with an overview page.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why give the report a `site` parameter rather than
copying it into five files, one per site?

**Answer.** Five copies drift. A fix to the denominator made in
one copy is missing from the other four, and nothing reports the
difference. With a parameter there is one source, so a correction
reaches every site's report at the next render.
:::

### Exercises

5. Give the worked example's report a `site` parameter that
   defaults to `"All"` and, when set, restricts `d` to that site.
   Render it for Site C and check the patient count against the
   data.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-11-5
site_report <- readLines(file.path(proj, "report.qmd"))
site_report <- append(site_report,
                      c("params:", '  site: "All"'), after = 3)
site_report <- sub(
  'd <- read.csv("data/trial.csv")',
  paste('d <- read.csv("data/trial.csv");',
        'if (params$site != "All") d <- d[d$site == params$site, ]'),
  site_report, fixed = TRUE
)
writeLines(site_report, file.path(proj, "report.qmd"))
site_c <- render_report(file.path(proj, "report.qmd"),
                        "-P", shQuote("site:Site C"))
site_c
stopifnot(grepl(sprintf("Of %d patients", sum(trial$site == "Site C")),
                site_c, fixed = TRUE))
```

The default `"All"` keeps the unparameterized render unchanged,
and the filter sits in the setup chunk, so every inline number
below it is computed for the chosen site. The `stopifnot()` is the
check: the count in the rendered sentence equals the count computed
from the data.
:::

## Reference: front matter and websites {#sec-quarto-reference}

### Front matter

The keys used in this chapter, with one example each:

| Key | Sets | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `title`, `author`, `date` | Title block | `date: today` |
| `format` | Output formats and their options | `html: {toc: true}`, `pdf: default` |
| `execute` | Defaults for every chunk | `echo: false`, `freeze: auto` |
| `bibliography`, `csl` | Citations and their style | `references.bib`, a CSL URL |
| `params` | Parameters and their defaults | `site: "All"` |

: Front-matter keys. Each format has many more options; the
Quarto reference for that format lists them. {#tbl-quarto-yaml}

Authors take a list of names with optional `affiliation` and
`orcid` fields. Format options nest under each format, so HTML and
PDF can have different figure sizes from one source.

### Websites

A directory of `.qmd` files governed by a `_quarto.yml` with
`project: type: website` renders to a website: linked pages with
shared navigation, theme, and search. This book is the same
machinery with `type: book`. The minimum is a `_quarto.yml`
naming the pages and an `index.qmd` landing page:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
website:
  title: "HF-HOME analysis"
  navbar:
    left: [index.qmd, methods.qmd, results.qmd]
```

`quarto render` builds the site into `_site/`, `quarto preview`
serves it with live reload, and `quarto publish gh-pages` (or
`netlify`, `quarto-pub`, `connect`) publishes it. For a research
team, a site is the natural form of an internal analysis portal:
it carries every guarantee of this chapter and is rebuilt on every
push by the CI workflow of @sec-ci, instead of being a PDF that is
emailed and goes stale.

## Float placement in PDF {#sec-rmd-workflow-floats}

The frustration: you cite a figure in your prose and it appears
two pages later. LaTeX treats figures and tables as [**floats**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-float)
and moves them to avoid awkward white space and bad page breaks.
For a paper, let it; readers expect floating figures. For a report
meant to be read top to bottom, force placement where the figure
is declared. The right default depends on the audience.

The fix in knitr Rmd:

````Rmd
```{{r demographics, fig.cap = "Demographics", fig.pos = "H"}}
plot(...)
```
````

Or globally:

```r
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.pos = "H")
```

In Quarto, `fig-pos` is a figure option rather than an
execution option, so it goes under the PDF format (or in a
single chunk as `#| fig-pos: "H"`):

```yaml
format:
  pdf:
    fig-pos: "H"
```

`H` is from the `float` LaTeX package, meaning 'place
exactly here, do not float'. Add to the YAML:

```yaml
header-includes:
  - \usepackage{float}
```

For tables, the equivalent is `tbl-pos: 'H'` in Quarto
or `kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")` in
knitr+kableExtra. @tbl-rmd-float-pos lists the placement codes.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `h` | Here, if possible |
| `t` | Top of a page |
| `b` | Bottom of a page |
| `p` | On a separate page of floats |
| `!` | Prefix: override LaTeX's usual limits on float placement |
| `H` | Exactly here, never float (requires the `float` package) |

: LaTeX float-placement codes. The default, `htbp`, lets LaTeX
choose among the first four in that order. {#tbl-rmd-float-pos}

For HTML output, float placement is irrelevant; figures appear in
source order.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You write 'Figure 3 shows demographics' and the
rendered PDF puts Figure 3 four pages later. Why, and what is the
fix?

**Answer.** LaTeX defers floats when placing them at the source
location would create awkward white space or break a paragraph,
sometimes by pages. Two fixes, best combined. Use `fig-pos: "H"`
(with `\usepackage{float}` in the header) to force exactly-here
placement, for documents that must be read linearly. And refer to
the figure by its cross-reference (`see @fig-demographics`) rather
than by a typed 'Figure 3', so that the number and the link are
correct wherever the figure lands.
:::

### Exercises

6. In a Quarto PDF with three tables, make every table appear
   exactly where it is declared.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Set the option once for the format and load the package:

```yaml
format:
  pdf:
    tbl-pos: "H"
header-includes:
  - \usepackage{float}
```

Verify in the PDF that each table follows the paragraph that
precedes it in the source. A table that still floats was probably
produced by a package that writes its own LaTeX float environment
(for example `kableExtra`), which needs that package's option
(`latex_options = "HOLD_position"`) instead.
:::

## Troubleshooting a render {#sec-rmd-workflow-troubleshoot}

A render fails in one of two ways. The loud failure stops it with
an error and a message that names the chunk; the silent failure
finishes, exits successfully, and leaves a defect in the output.
@tbl-rmd-render-failures collects the common ones; the worked
example after it shows how to read a real log.

| Symptom (message excerpt) | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Error: ! object 'x' not found`, then `Quitting from doc.qmd:14-18 [label]` | The object is created in a chunk that did not run (`eval: false`, or deleted) or runs later | Read the `Quitting from` line for the failing chunk; make the defining chunk run, and run before it |
| `could not find function` | A package is used but not loaded in the document | Add the `library()` call to the document's setup chunk; the render runs in a fresh session |
| `Unable to resolve crossref @fig-x` (a warning), and `?@fig-x` in the output | A missing or misspelled label, a label without its `fig-` or `tbl-` prefix, or a chunk that did not run | Fix the label; grep the output for `?@` (@sec-rmd-workflow-migrate) |
| `\@ref(fig:x)` printed literally in the output | A `bookdown` reference left unconverted | Rewrite as `@fig-x` (@tbl-rmd-vs-quarto) |
| `No TeX installation was detected` | PDF output needs LaTeX | `quarto install tinytex` |
| `LaTeX Error: File ... .sty not found` | A LaTeX package missing from a minimal TeX installation | Install it (`tinytex::tlmgr_install("float")`, with the package's name), or let TinyTeX install it on the next render |
| `ModuleNotFoundError` in a Python chunk | Python packages not declared | `reticulate::py_require()` (@sec-rmd-workflow-engines) |
| `unknown writer` or an unknown format | A misspelled `format:` name, or a Quarto older than the format | Check the name; run `quarto check` and update Quarto |
| Figures pages away from their citation | LaTeX float placement | `fig-pos` (@sec-rmd-workflow-floats) |
| Every render slow | Expensive chunks re-run every time | `freeze` or `cache` (@sec-quarto-freeze) |
| Old numbers after new data | `freeze` or `cache` served stored results | Render the document itself (@sec-quarto-freeze) |

: Common rendering failures. The first two block the render; the
next two finish with a defect in the output. {#tbl-rmd-render-failures}

### Worked example: a render that fails, then succeeds wrongly

The example renders a one-figure HF-HOME report, from the `trial`
table of @sec-quarto-worked, in a temporary directory, with two
defects planted from real conversions: a setup
chunk left at `eval: false` from drafting, and a figure label that
kept its R Markdown name. It runs the real `quarto` command, so
the log below is what you would see.[^r-libs]

[^r-libs]: As in the earlier worked example, the `env` argument passes
    this session's library paths to the R process that Quarto
    starts. In a terminal you would type `quarto render report.qmd`
    alone.

```{r}
#| label: rmd-debug-setup
dbg <- file.path(tempdir(), "debug")
unlink(dbg, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(dbg)
write.csv(trial[c("patient_id", "arm", "event_30d")],
          file.path(dbg, "trial.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

doc <- c(
  "---", "title: 'HF-HOME: primary outcome'", "format: gfm", "---",
  "",
  "```{r}",
  "#| label: setup",
  "#| eval: false",
  "d <- read.csv('trial.csv')",
  "obs <- d[!is.na(d$event_30d), ]",
  "risk <- 100 * tapply(obs$event_30d, obs$arm, mean)",
  "```",
  "",
  "@fig-risk shows the observed risk in each arm.",
  "",
  "```{r}",
  "#| label: risk",
  "#| fig-cap: 'Observed 30-day risk by arm'",
  "barplot(risk, ylab = 'Risk (%)')",
  "```"
)

render_doc <- function(doc) {
  writeLines(doc, file.path(dbg, "report.qmd"))
  r_libs <- paste0("R_LIBS=",
                   paste(.libPaths(), collapse = .Platform$path.sep))
  log <- suppressWarnings(system2(
    "quarto", c("render", file.path(dbg, "report.qmd")),
    stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE, env = r_libs
  ))
  status <- if (is.null(attr(log, "status"))) 0 else attr(log, "status")
  log <- gsub("\033\\[[0-9;]*m", "", log)
  log <- sub("^WARNING \\(.*\\) ", "WARNING ", log)
  list(status = status,
       log = grep("Error|^!|Quitting|WARN", log, value = TRUE))
}
```

Render it:

```{r}
#| label: rmd-debug-first
first <- render_doc(doc)
first
```

The render failed (a non-zero status), and the log says why in
two lines. Read it from the bottom up. `Quitting from` names the
file, the source lines, and the chunk label of the chunk that
failed, here `risk`; the error above it names what that chunk
could not find. The object is defined in `setup`, which never ran.
The fix is to let it run:

```{r}
#| label: rmd-debug-second
doc <- doc[doc != "#| eval: false"]
second <- render_doc(doc)
second
```

The status is now zero, and a build script or continuous
integration would report success. The log still carries a
warning: `risk` is not a figure label, because it lacks the
`fig-` prefix, so the reference in the prose resolved to nothing.
Look at the sentence Quarto wrote:

```{r}
#| label: rmd-debug-second-output
grep("shows the observed", readLines(file.path(dbg, "report.md")),
     value = TRUE)
```

This is the silent failure, and it is the more expensive of the
two: the first defect stopped the render, and this one shipped.
Rename the label:

```{r}
#| label: rmd-debug-third
doc <- sub("#| label: risk", "#| label: fig-risk", doc, fixed = TRUE)
third <- render_doc(doc)
third
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
A render is done when the status is zero, the log has no warning,
and the output contains no unresolved reference.

```{r}
#| label: rmd-debug-verify
out <- readLines(file.path(dbg, "report.md"))
stopifnot(
  third$status == 0,
  length(grep("WARN", third$log)) == 0,
  !any(grepl("?@", out, fixed = TRUE))
)
grep("shows the observed", out, value = TRUE)
```

The first two conditions are the log; the third is the output,
and it is the one that would have caught a converted paper sent
to co-authors with `?@fig-flow` in its methods section
(@sec-rmd-workflow).
:::

When a failure is not in @tbl-rmd-render-failures, reduce it.
Copy the document, delete chunks and prose until the error
disappears, and restore the last thing you deleted; what remains
is a minimal example, usually under twenty lines, that either
shows you the cause or is ready to post to the Quarto discussion
forum. `quarto check` reports the versions of Quarto, R, knitr,
and LaTeX that belong in any such post.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A model is good at reading a render log, provided you give it the
right excerpt and forbid the fixes that hide the error.

> **Context.** A Quarto document fails to render. Below are the
> last 30 lines of the log, the chunk named in the `Quitting
> from` line with the chunks before it that define its inputs,
> and the output of `quarto check`.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not suggest `error: true`, `eval: false`,
> `warning: false`, `try()`, or reinstalling Quarto or R unless
> the log shows a version problem. Change as few lines as
> possible.
>
> **Criteria.** Name the line that fails and the cause, and say
> what the log shows that supports the diagnosis. After your fix,
> the render exits with status zero, the log has no `WARN` line,
> and the output contains no `?@`.

*Failure mode.* The suggested fix silences the symptom, by
skipping the chunk or tolerating the error, and turns a loud
failure into a silent one. *Check.* Apply the fix, re-render, and
run this section's Verification on the output. A log and chunk
code are structure; if the error message prints data values, cut
them before sending (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In the debugging example, the second render exited
with status zero. Why is a zero status not enough to call a render
correct, and what two further checks does the Verification add?

**Answer.** A zero status means the document compiled. Quarto
treats an unresolved cross-reference as a warning, so a document
can reach a reader with `?@fig-risk` in its prose and a successful
build behind it. The Verification also requires a log with no
warning and an output with no `?@`.
:::

### Exercises

7. A render log ends with these lines. Which chunk failed, what is
   the likely cause, and where do you look first?

```
4/9 [fit-model]
Error:
! object 'analysis_set' not found
Quitting from paper.qmd:61-70 [fit-model]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The chunk labeled `fit-model`, at lines 61 to 70 of `paper.qmd`,
uses `analysis_set` before anything has created it. Look first at
the chunk that should define `analysis_set`: it is set to
`eval: false`, it comes after `fit-model`, or it was deleted. If
the document reads `analysis_set` from a file or a pipeline
target, check that the reading chunk ran.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 10: every number in the prose is computed.** Sample
   sizes, estimates, intervals, and p-values are inline
   expressions, and figures and tables are cross-referenced by
   label.
2. **Habit 8: a stale number is a plausible number, and a clean
   render is not a correct render.** `freeze` and `cache` watch
   code, not data; after a data change, render the document itself
   and check the counts it reports. A zero exit status means the
   document compiled; grep the output for `?@` as well.
3. **Habit 2: the rendered document is a build product.** Never
   edit the `.html`, `.pdf`, or `.docx`; change the source and
   render again.

## Cumulative practice

8. *Cumulative (uses @sec-joins).* Rebuild the worked example's
   `trial` table with `dplyr::left_join()`, declaring the
   relationship and refusing unmatched keys, and assert that it has
   one row per randomized patient. Explain why the report's first
   number depends on this join being right.
9. *On your own work (no key).* Replace every typed number in a
   draft of yours with inline code. Render it, render it again
   against deliberately different data, and confirm that every
   number changed.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 8'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-11-6
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

trial_joined <- randomization |>
  select(patient_id, site, rand_date, arm) |>
  left_join(select(outcomes, patient_id, event_30d),
            by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "one-to-one", unmatched = "error")
stopifnot(nrow(trial_joined) == nrow(randomization),
          identical(sort(trial_joined$patient_id),
                    sort(trial$patient_id)))
nrow(trial_joined)
```

The report's first sentence counts the rows of `trial.csv`, so a
join that dropped patients would shrink the denominator, and one
that multiplied them would inflate it, while the sentence went on
rendering a plausible number. Declaring the relationship and the
unmatched behavior makes either failure stop the build.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Render a document | `quarto render report.qmd` | A stale output (always executes) |
| Render a project | `quarto render` | Inconsistent pages (respects `freeze`) |
| Put a number in a sentence | `` `{{r}} nrow(d)` `` | Numbers typed from the console |
| Refer to a figure | `@fig-label` | 'Figure 3' pointing at the wrong figure |
| Cite a work | `[@key]` | Hand-typed, unformattable references |
| Reuse a whole document's results | `execute: freeze: auto` | Re-running a slow analysis on every project render |
| Reuse one chunk's result | `cache: true` | Re-running one slow chunk |
| Re-run a cached chunk when data change | `cache.extra: !expr tools::md5sum("data/x.csv")` | A cache that does not see the data |
| Render one variant | `quarto render report.qmd -P site:"Site C"` | Five drifting copies of one report |
| Force a figure in place (PDF) | `fig-pos: "H"` with `\usepackage{float}` | A figure pages away from its citation |
| Force a table in place (PDF) | `tbl-pos: "H"` | A table pages away from its citation |
| Find unresolved references | `grep -rn '?@' _book/` | A clean render with broken references |
| Report versions for a bug report | `quarto check` | A bug report no one can reproduce |

: Quarto at a glance. {#tbl-quarto-cheat-sheet}

## Further reading

- The Quarto documentation at `quarto.org`, the canonical
  reference, in particular the guides to computations and to
  managing execution (freeze and cache).
- [@wickham2023r4ds] Chapters 28 and 29, Quarto and its output
  formats.
- [@knuth1984literate], the paper that named the idea this
  chapter implements.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-11}

1. Literate programming (coined by Knuth) interleaves code with the
   prose that explains it, so the same source file is the
   authoritative record of both the computation and its
   interpretation. A Quarto `.qmd` file embodies this by letting
   you write narrative Markdown and executable R (or Python,
   Julia) code chunks in one document. The render process produces
   a human-readable artifact (HTML, PDF, Word) with code, output,
   and prose interleaved.
2. `quarto render file.qmd` produces the default output format
   declared in the document's YAML `format:` key (HTML if no
   `format:` is present). To force a format, use
   `quarto render file.qmd --to html` (or `--to pdf`,
   `--to docx`).
3. In a Quarto project, `execute: freeze: auto` stores each
   document's executed results in `_freeze/` when the project is
   rendered. Later project renders reuse them for every document
   whose source is unchanged, and re-execute a document in full
   when any part of it changes, avoiding re-running expensive code
   on every render and making CI deployments fast. It does not
   apply to a single-file render, which always executes, and the
   default is `freeze: false`. Commit `_freeze/` to Git so
   collaborators benefit from it.
4. LaTeX treats figures and tables as floats and rearranges them
   by default to avoid bad page breaks. `fig-pos: 'H'` (requires
   the `float` package) and `tbl-pos: 'H'` in Quarto YAML tell
   LaTeX 'place this exactly here, no reflow'. The default
   placement, `htbp`, means 'try here, then top, then bottom, then
   a float page' in order.
